analysis.one_liner: Requires background checks for nearly all firearm sales, including those between private individuals.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the Senate before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for private individuals to sell or transfer a firearm without a licensed dealer first running a background check, with exceptions for gifts within families, hunting, target shooting, self-defense transfers, and certain estate inheritances [S2][S3]. It was introduced by Senator Chris Murphy in October 2017 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it stalled without any hearings or votes [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people are the intended beneficiaries: the bill aimed to keep firearms away from people prohibited from owning them (felons, domestic abusers, etc.) by closing the so-called private-sale loophole. Under current law, private sales between individuals don't require background checks, so prohibited buyers can purchase guns from private sellers with no check [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents in states without universal checks

how_it_helps.text: Closes the private-sale loophole by requiring that a licensed dealer conduct a background check before any private firearm transfer [S2][S3].

Includes targeted exemptions to preserve common transfers: gifts between spouses, parents, children, siblings, grandparents, and aunts/uncles to nieces/nephews; estate and trust transfers; temporary transfers to prevent imminent death; and transfers for hunting, target shooting, or while in the transferor's presence [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private gun sellers would need to route sales through licensed dealers, who charge a fee for running background checks, adding cost and time to private transactions. Licensed dealers would gain business from the mandate. Gun owners transferring within the enumerated family or hunting exceptions would face no new requirements [S3].

drawbacks.text: Private sellers and buyers would pay dealer transfer fees and navigate dealer logistics for every private sale, a real cost in rural areas with few nearby licensed dealers [S3].

Opponents of universal background checks argue such laws are difficult to enforce between private parties and may not meaningfully reduce crime, since criminals obtain firearms through theft or straw purchases rather than documented sales. The bill contains no provisions addressing this enforcement critique.

The bill defines exceptions narrowly, so some lawful transfers outside the listed family relationships (e.g., friends, cousins) would still require dealer involvement even where the parties know each other well [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core policy goal—closing the private-sale background check gap—is broadly supported in public polling, and the exemptions for family gifts, hunting, and self-defense address many practical objections. The main costs are transaction fees and inconvenience for private sellers and buyers, plus the persistent question of enforceability between individuals. The bill is a straightforward, if narrow, expansion of an existing system rather than a sweeping new regime.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in October 2017, the bill sat there for the rest of the 115th Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on October 25, 2017, with 30 original Democratic cosponsors [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action was taken for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
The bill accumulated 40 cosponsors (39 Democrats and 1 Independent) but no Republican support, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one acted on it, so the status quo persisted: private sales between individuals remained exempt from background checks, which gun-rights groups and private sellers preferred. People hoping for universal checks gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: private sellers and gun-rights groups

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and recruited 30 original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 40 Senate cosponsors (39 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it full Democratic conference support but no Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill—no hearing, no markup, no vote—after referral in October 2017.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party control of the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor consideration; as majority leader, Sen. Mitch McConnell controlled which bills reached the floor, and this one never did.

against.name: Republican senators
against.role: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill
against.what_they_did: Offered zero cosponsorship, signaling no appetite to move the bill through committee or onto the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Senator Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee and Senate leadership never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Every private sale would have to route through a licensed dealer, who charges a fee for the transfer and background check, creating a new revenue stream. Dealers were the bill's mechanism rather than its target.

industries.industry: Gun manufacturing and retail (NRA-aligned gun industry)
industries.note: The industry and its advocacy groups generally oppose universal background check mandates as a precedent for further regulation and an added cost to sales channels. The bill would not ban any firearm, but the private-sale exemption from checks—which the industry benefits from—would end.
Individuals selling firearms privately would lose the ability to complete a sale without a dealer intermediary and its fees.
